# Feature development

## When to use

In the `planning` and `implementation` phases of the feature workflow, and for any other
change that adds or alters behavior. For restructuring without behavior change use
`refactoring`; for throwaway exploration use `prototyping`.

## Required context

None beyond the code. Useful when present: the feature map entry for the area, the
architecture context (boundaries), the rules in scope and the verification profile, to
know which checks exist before promising any.

## Preconditions

- The requirement can be written as observable claims ("given X, the system does Y").
  If it cannot, ask; do not fill gaps in a requirement with guesses.
- The affected code and the pattern to follow are known. If not, activate
  `context-discovery` first.

## Procedure

1. **Understand the requirement.** Write it as claims, including the edge cases the
   requirement implies (empty input, missing data, limits, failure of a dependency).
   List what is out of scope.
2. **Locate the affected code** through the feature map or by following the entry point
   of the behavior. Name every file you expect to change.
   For technology-specific code, read the relevant knowledge under the selected
   adapter in the pinned Core runtime; use the project's adapter selection, and do not
   apply guidance from an unselected technology.
3. **Plan the proof.** For each claim, pick the check type from the profile that will
   prove it. A claim no check can prove gets a planned artifact and a gap, decided now,
   not after the code is written.
4. **Choose the working capacity.** Use the lightest available model that can handle
   each bounded task reliably. Reserve stronger models for ambiguous requirements,
   architecture choices, difficult debugging, security-sensitive reasoning and final
   synthesis. Use cheaper, faster models for mechanical edits, narrow research, test
   drafting and independent checks when their output is easy to verify. Model names and
   capabilities vary by host; inspect its available choices instead of assuming a fixed
   catalog, and do not spend tokens asking a model to repeat context another session
   already has.
5. **Delegate only independent work.** Split work when tasks have clear inputs and
   outputs, can proceed without editing the same files or waiting on each other, and the
   expected time saved exceeds the cost of starting and coordinating sessions. Give each
   session a narrow brief with relevant context, expected result and constraints. Use
   separate sessions for parallel research, isolated test work or independent review;
   keep shared-state edits and tightly coupled reasoning in one session. Limit concurrent
   sessions to what the host and task can usefully support.
   When delegation will save time, register a machine-readable graph with
   `paved delegation plan --run <id> --file <graph.yaml> --json`, bound to the approved
   plan digest. Include task dependencies, exact read/write paths, output contracts and
   model policy. Keep concurrent write scopes disjoint. Use
   `paved delegation ready --run <id> --json` to see what can start. Show the complete
   graph to the user and obtain explicit approval before `paved delegation approve
   --run <id> --approve --json`; approval is tied to the immutable graph digest.
   Start work only after approval. Paved validates
   and records the graph; the active host owns native agent/session creation and work.
   Use Claude Code's native subagents when available. In Codex, use native collaboration
   tools when available and account for delegated agents inheriting the parent model and
   execution environment when the host offers no per-task routing. Inspect the host's
   actual model and reasoning controls; map `economy`, `balanced` and `frontier` to its
   lightest suitable options rather than assuming a fixed model catalog. Keep stronger
   capacity for ambiguity, architecture, difficult debugging and security-sensitive
   tasks. Treat requested reasoning effort as guidance if the host cannot honor it.
   Ask `paved delegation capabilities --host <claude-code|codex>` for host guidance.
   Claude Code subagents support per-invocation model and effort selection; prefer
   isolated worktrees for parallel edits. Codex routing and isolation depend on the
   active host configuration. Host permissions remain authoritative. Start with
   `--isolation shared-workspace` or `--isolation isolated-worktree`; shared-workspace
   writers are serialized. Record the actual host/model/effort with
   `paved delegation start`; after the host
   reports completion, save a concise result under
   `.paved/generated/delegation-results/<run-id>/` and use `paved delegation finish`
   with the result path, outcome, each changed path via repeated `--changed-path`, and
   available usage. Paved checks reported paths against exact write scopes; paths from
   isolated worktrees remain host-reported and require primary-agent diff inspection.
   For an interrupted session, verify it has stopped before
   `paved delegation recover --run <id> --task <id> --confirmed-stopped --note <reason>`.
   Recovery preserves the attempt and makes it retryable. Usage is host-reported, not
   independently verified. Never store prompts, credentials or raw session ids. Keep
   short, tightly dependent or shared-file tasks in the primary session when startup
   and coordination cost exceeds the likely time saved.
6. **Integrate centrally.** The primary agent owns the approved plan, resolves conflicting
   results, checks delegated changes against the plan and repository state, and remains
   responsible for tests, verification, evidence and completion. A delegated result is
   input, not proof: inspect its diff and rerun affected checks. Do not let parallel work
   bypass approvals or change scope without updating the plan.
7. **Implement in small steps** that mirror the chosen sibling: naming, structure, error
   handling, logging, configuration. The diff contains only what the claims need.
8. **Add tests with the code.** Hand the tests for each level to its skill:
   `unit-testing` for logic, `integration-testing` for boundaries with real
   collaborators, `e2e-testing` when the claim is a user-visible flow.
9. **Run the fast checks** after each meaningful step and fix failures before going on.
10. **Clean up** imports, parameters, files and flags the change left unused.
11. **Self-review** the diff with `core.repository.diff`, and confirm with `core.repository.status` that
   no unintended file changed.
12. **Verify and record** every required check, then hand over to the `verification` phase.

For a Paved workflow, keep the durable plan at
`.paved/documents/plans/<run-id>.md`. Put a behavior contract in
`.paved/documents/specs/<run-id>.md` when the requirement needs one, and a task breakdown
in `.paved/documents/tasks/<run-id>.md` when it helps execute the plan. Use the same
workflow run id in related filenames and follow `core.instructions.workflows` for review.

## Tools

`core.repository.diff` for self-review; `core.repository.status` for unintended files. Build and test
commands come from the Tools named by Checks in the verification profile.

## Rules

`core.architecture.follow-existing-patterns` and
`core.architecture.respect-declared-boundaries` shape steps 2 and 4.
`core.security.no-secrets-in-source` covers test data and examples as well as code.
`core.quality.evidence-before-completion` governs step 9.

## Verification

Required: `unit`. Recommended when the profile has them: `build` and `static-analysis`
(they validate, but prove no behavior), `integration` for changed boundaries, `e2e` for
changed user flows.

## Evidence

A check result for every claim, the diff, and a gap for each claim without an
available check.

## Completion criteria

- Every claim has a passed check or a supporting artifact, or is an explained gap.
- The diff touches only files named in step 2, or the plan was updated to say why.
- No new static-analysis warnings in the changed files.

## Failure modes

| Failure | Signal | Response |
|---|---|---|
| Scope creep | Diff touches files unrelated to the claims | Revert the unrelated parts |
| New pattern by accident | Code differs in style from its siblings | Rewrite to match, or record why not |
| Proof chosen after the fact | Claims appear only after implementation | Re-plan the claims; confirm the tests assert them |
| Requirement grows during work | New claims appear mid-implementation | Stop and confirm them with a human |

## References

None.


## Paved integration

Use the project-local Paved contract as the source of truth. Discover state with `node "<plugin root>/scripts/paved.mjs" status --json`, load only relevant `.paved/project/` context, and invoke verification with `node "<plugin root>/scripts/paved.mjs" verify --json`. `<plugin root>` is the installed Paved plugin directory, two directories above this SKILL.md. Always run the launcher from the repository being worked on, never from the plugin directory. Do not edit generated integration files or bypass Paved lifecycle and ownership checks.
